title: Australian wine exports drop to 22-year low
summary:
Australian wine exports have fallen to their lowest level in more than two decades as a worldwide decline in wine consumption weighs on demand, according to a new industry report.

The post Australian wine exports drop to 22-year low appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Australian wine exports have fallen to their lowest level in more than two decades as a worldwide decline in wine consumption weighs on demand, according to a new industry report. Exports dropped 7% in value to A$2.3bn (£1.1bn) and 6% in volume to 598 million litres in the year to June 2026, industry body Wine Australia has revealed in its annual Export Report, released today. It is the first time export volumes have fallen below 600 million litres since 2004. The decline comes amid a broader slowdown in global wine consumption, which Wine Australia says has fallen to its lowest level since 1961. The industry attributes the trend to changing consumer habits, cost-of-living pressures and growing demand for alternative alcoholic beverages. Australia's three largest export markets, which are mainland China, the United Kingdom and the United States, all posted declines over the past year. Wine Australia manager market insights Peter Bailey said the challenges facing Australian exporters reflected wider changes across the global wine industry. "Data from multiple sources suggests the decline in wine consumption globally is more than a short-term downturn — it's a reflection of changing consumer behaviour that is reshaping demand around the world," he said. Bailey said the shift highlighted the importance of understanding changing consumer preferences and identifying markets where demand remained strong.

China slowdown after tariff recovery

Mainland China remained Australia's largest export market by value despite a 15% decline to A$756m. Wine Australia said the fall followed the end of the initial recovery period after Chinese tariffs on Australian wine were lifted, with the market now entering what it described as a more mature phase driven by underlying consumer demand rather than stock replenishment. Bailey said Australia continued to be the leading supplier of imported wine to China despite the weaker sales.

UK and US exports decline

The United Kingdom remained Australia's largest market by export volume, while the United States ranked second. However, shipments to both countries fell to their lowest levels in 25 years. Wine Australia said weaker sales in the UK were concentrated in lower and mid-priced wines, while premium Australian wines had proved more resilient. In the United States, the report pointed to softer demand across most price categories, citing declining wine consumption, stronger competition from domestic and international producers, lower retailer inventories and changing consumer preferences.

Canada and Asia record growth

Despite the broader downturn, several markets posted strong gains. Exports to Canada rose 20% in value to A$188m and 13% in volume, reaching their highest value in seven years. Wine Australia said the increase was partly driven by market-share gains following reduced availability of US wines during the Canada-US trade dispute, although growth slowed towards the end of the reporting period. Several Asian markets outside mainland China also recorded higher exports, including Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. Singapore became Australia's largest Asian export market outside mainland China, while Thailand achieved record export values, driven by demand for premium Australian wines.

title: ‘Worst crisis since WWII’: Bordeaux wildfires continue amid extreme heat
summary:
As wildfires continue to blaze near Bordeaux, in what President Emmanuel Macron has described as the toughest situation France has faced since World War II, the country's celebrated wine region confronts a growing environmental crisis.

The post ‘Worst crisis since WWII’: Bordeaux wildfires continue amid extreme heat appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
As wildfires continue to blaze near Bordeaux, in what President Emmanuel Macron has described as the toughest situation France has faced since World War II, the country's celebrated wine region confronts a growing environmental crisis. Thousands of firefighters are working around the clock to contain one of the largest fires in modern French history in the Gironde region, home to many of the many famed vineyards of Bordeaux. The blazes have forced more than 220,000 people to evacuate across France and destroyed around 240 homes, according to officials. Of this number, around 4,000 people have also been evacuated from tourist hotspots along France's Atlantic coast, including campsites and holiday villages. The French government has urged tourists to avoid the Bordeaux area, dealing a fresh blow to the region's tourism industry at the height of the summer season. The timing could hardly be worse for Bordeaux’s wine sector, adding to challenges it is currently facing – from falling consumption to wider economic pressures.  Wine tourism was a bright spot, but now, the wildfires have pulled the stops on the growing sector. "Tourism was really the only dynamic part of the business that was still growing, both for us and, more generally, for Bordeaux wines," winemaker Edouard Le Grix de la Salle told The Independent. "And now this comes along as a brake." Le Grix de la Salle criticised the authorities for failing to better protect one of the region's most valuable industries. "How did they not think about protecting that sector? And the cultural sector, too. There's so much to visit in Bordeaux. There are so many museums, there are châteaux. It's unbelievable," he said. Peggy Plouhinec, general director of Château Picque Caillou, one of the few wine estates on Bordeaux's western side, added that her estate had temporarily closed because of heavy smoke. "The hospitality sector will be impacted this summer, that's for sure," she told BBC. "What is happening is unprecedented. We're lucky that we haven't been too affected yet, but the business will still suffer from the lower numbers of tourists." She said conditions had improved following rainfall on Sunday night,

Climate pressures mount

While vineyard owners say most vines have evaded direct damage from the flames, the fires have intensified concerns about the long-term effects of climate change on Bordeaux's vineyards. The region has endured months of intense heat and severe drought, leaving vegetation tinder dry and fuelling the spread of wildfires while placing vineyards under increasing water stress. In Margaux, where some of Bordeaux's most prestigious wines are produced, vines remain intact and wine quality is not currently expected to suffer as a direct result of the fires, according to Thomas Duroux, director general of Château Palmer. However, he warned that this year's conditions marked a turning point. "What we are experiencing this year is a wake-up call. We are facing something we have never seen before. We not only have to limit the damage, but also look to the future," he said. "Our priorities today are water resources – because without water we will no longer be able to plant vines in conditions like these – and adapting our vineyard so it becomes more resilient to these climatic conditions." Duroux acknowledged that climate change has brought some benefits to Bordeaux in recent years, including riper grapes and richer wines during particularly hot vintages such as 2020, 2022 and 2025. But he warned that without significant rainfall in the coming weeks, vines could shut down to conserve water, causing grapes to shrivel and reducing both yields and quality.

The smoke taint debate

Attention is also turning to the risk of "smoke taint", a controversial issue in the wine world. Smoke taint occurs when compounds released by wildfire smoke are absorbed into grape skins. During red wine fermentation, these compounds can be extracted from the skins, potentially giving wines undesirable smoky, ashy or medicinal flavours. The extent of the risk depends on factors including the vineyard's proximity to the fire, the density and duration of smoke exposure, and the stage of grape development. Posting on LinkedIn, wine brand creator and consultant Robert Joseph warned that vineyards within 50 to 100 kilometres downwind of major fires should be monitored closely. "For Bordeaux in late July, with véraison beginning, vineyards lying anywhere within 50–100 km downwind of a substantial fire are worth monitoring or testing," he wrote. "A 20 km or even 50 km separation should not automatically reassure growers if fresh smoke has remained over the vines for several hours,” he added. Red Bordeaux varieties may also reveal the problem more strongly because red-wine fermentation extracts smoke-derived compounds from the skins." Winemaker Sally Evans echoed those concerns. "We have woken up to smoke again this morning after a couple of days' respite. The difficulty is the fact that this can reveal itself so far down the line – post fermentation and even after some time in bottle. "The possible risk may encourage even more of us to make some Blanc de Noir this year given it is the skin contact which is the most problematic... already in the plan for this year but maybe we should make more than had planned." However, Colin Hay, the drinks business' Bordeaux correspondent, urged caution against drawing premature conclusions. "There's very little established scientific evidence to date of smoke taint being passed to vines that are not in close proximity to the fire itself — and at present the nearest vineyards are at around 15km from the source of the smoke to which they are exposed," he told db. "Some vineyards are geographically closer, but the smoke they have experienced has come from further away due to the prevailing wind direction." Hay said Bordeaux's experience during the 2022 wildfires offered some reassurance. "There were certainly anxieties then and much talk of smoke taint. But in the end any suggestion of smoke taint in the wines vinified was restricted to some isolated parcels in the Graves that were never used in the final blend and that came from parcels directly adjacent to the fire itself." He added that the unusual conditions of the 2026 growing season could also reduce the immediate risk. "Many vines, suffering as they are from a combination of thermal and hydric stress, are in a current stage of blockage, with the bunches essentially stuck at 10-20% of véraison. Physiologically not much is happening and that is likely to reduce any absorption of smoke for now at least."

title: Could chilled reds be a premium move?
summary:
As luxury store Fortnum & Mason unveils a new collection of chilled reds to meet the viral trend, senior wine buyer Edwina Watson tells Sarah Neish why drinking reds cool "still feels counterintuitive to many" and how getting it right requires focusing on "style rather than quality or price point".

The post Could chilled reds be a premium move? appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
As luxury store Fortnum & Mason unveils a new collection of chilled reds to meet the viral trend, senior wine buyer Edwina Watson tells Sarah Neish why drinking reds cool "still feels counterintuitive to many" and how getting it right requires focusing on "style rather than quality or price point". It's no secret that global sales of red wine have been dwindling as consumers' eyes swivel towards lighter bodied, lower alcohol, and often white expressions. But could chilled reds be the answer to producers' prayers? It seems so. As db revealed last month, online searches for 'chilled reds' surged between February and June 2026, according to Google's 'Summergeist' report on the biggest trends of the season. And online explorers were no longer asking "should I drink red wine chilled?" but rather seeking information on which red wines taste best chilled, signalling a change in the wind towards the serving style.

Bordeaux gets on board

What's more, Bordeaux is reviving its historic ‘claret’ name for a new category of light, fruit-forward, chillable dry red wines aimed at attracting younger consumers back to the region. All grape varieties are permitted in the new Bordeaux Claret, effective from the 2025 vintage, in which short maceration of two to four days produces lightly coloured, low-tannin, unoaked wines intended to be served chilled.  Focused on the on-trade, Bordeaux Claret wines are even recommended to be poured over ice. The building momentum was solidified when luxury UK department store Fortnum & Mason announced this week that it is launching a new range of own-label 'chilled reds'. Speaking exclusively to db, Fortnum's senior wine buyer Edwina Watson said that "as a retailer of premium wines, we wanted to respond to market changes in a way that allows customers to explore something new, while not forgetting the classics."

Pendulum swing

Of course serving red wine chilled is nothing new in Mediterranean countries such as Spain and Italy where refrigerated reds have long been sipped on sunny terraces, but for some components of the UK trade it has, until fairly recently, been seen as sacrilegious to serve a bottle of red at anything cooler than room temperature. Is climate change responsible for the pendulum swing? "As UK summers have become warmer, it is perhaps unsurprising that customers are looking to enjoy lighter-bodied chilled red wines, in a way that is the norm in Italy or Spain," said Watson. "The traditional maxim of 'room temperature' for red wines is really too warm in a heatwave, or in our centrally heated homes, so the concept of 'chilled reds' is a helpful way to communicate how to best enjoy certain red wines."

Global spread

From a retail perspective, "clear merchandising and communication" is needed to help customers discover wines they may have previously overlooked through the medium of chilling them. The Fortnum's own-label range includes bottles priced from £13.95 to £29.95 and encompasses quality expressions spanning Beaujolais and Valpolicella to Garnacha, Monastrell, Dão and Tempranillo. "Each bottle has been carefully selected to be enjoyed lightly chilled, bringing out their bright fruit, freshness and versatility," explained Fortnum's, which has also implemented a new 'chilled reds' section on its website, suggesting options outside of the store's own-label range that the buying team believes are perfect for chilling. This larger portfolio include a 'Rosso' from Etna, a Pinot Noir from South Africa, a Xinomavro from Naoussa in northern Greece and a Blaufrankisch from Burgenland in eastern Austria, as well as an intriguing English red from Norfolk made from Pinot Précoce. "The interest in chilled reds reflects how we have been developing our buying strategy, towards a contemporary range that includes fresh, elegant and versatile styles of reds," said Watson.

Education piece

Not all UK consumers will be familiar with what makes a red wine 'chillable'. Will there be an education piece from Fortnum's explaining how to enjoy the new range and what temperature to serve it at?

"The idea of a 'chilled red' can still feel counterintuitive to many customers," said Watson. "Our advice is simple but not prescriptive: these wines are best served lightly chilled, around 10–14°C, rather than fridge-cold. We want customers to be aware that it’s about enhancing freshness and aromatics, not making a wine so cold that it masks its character."

When choosing which bottles to include in the range, Watson told db that the team had looked for wines with "bright acidity, vibrant fruit, balanced alcohol and supple tannins." She added: "These types of wine are even more expressive when served slightly chilled."

Quality perception

One obstacle to sale could be the entrenched perception that only lower quality reds should be served chilled. Many UK wine lovers would recoil in horror, for instance, at the idea of chilling a Super Tuscan or first-growth Bordeaux. Watson is clear on this point. "Serving temperature is about style rather than quality or price point," she said. "Some of the world’s finest lighter-bodied reds are delicious served with a slight chill because cooler temperatures can emphasise the aromatics and detail in a wine. Whether a wine costs £15 or £50, the right serving temperature helps to show it at its best." She stressed that "we want to help customers understand that serving temperature should complement a wine’s style, rather than compensate for its quality." Ultimately, Watson is keen to dispel the notion of chilled reds as a gimmick. "I think it’s encouraging that customers are interested in the concept as it indicates a curiosity around how and when to enjoy wine, rather than thinking of chilled reds simply as a novelty," she said. "And we have plenty to offer in this category, not limited to a particular grape variety or region."

title: Younger Bordeaux vintages drive record year at iDealwine
summary:
In what was a "record year" for iDealwine, co-founder of the online auction business Angélique de Lencquesaing told db in a podcast last week that Bordeaux had seen a "big rise" in 2025.

The post Younger Bordeaux vintages drive record year at iDealwine appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
In what was a "record year" for iDealwine, co-founder of the online auction business Angélique de Lencquesaing told db in a podcast last week that Bordeaux had seen a "big rise" in 2025.

During an interview on 23 July – which you can listen to below – de Lencquesaing said that her business, which has offices in Paris, Hong Kong, Singapore and New York, had seen a 9% increase in value, and 19% of volumes sales passing through its auctions.

According to iDealwine's Auction Barometer report, that meant a total of almost 391,000 bottles, representing €33.9 million (€42.4m including fees).

Notably, despite the ongoing news of Bordeaux oversupply and vineyard removal schemes, iDealwine saw Bordeaux volumes up 23% (105,000+ bottles – one in three lots sold), with the Barometer showing value sales increasing by 19% to €12.5m, and prices remaining almost flat (-3% vs. the market's -8%).

A big interest in Bordeaux

Commenting on the trend, she said, "It's quite amazing: everyone is talking about Bordeaux being completely out of fashion, but that has never been true on iDealwine, actually, and last year we saw that people have a big interest in Bordeaux."

Continuing she recorded, "What I think is quite interesting and also quite a surprise is that younger vintages are trading more actively."

Putting numbers to the latter observation, she said, "Bordeaux wines that are under 10 years old represented 28% of the bottles that were auctioned last year, and the year before, it was only 20% – so it was a very, very big increase in younger wines."

Explaining the development, she said, "I think it's a result of the change that has occurred on the style of the wines that are produced in Bordeaux, which makes them accessible younger; they can be drunk younger."

She added, "People now know that they won't have to wait for decades before they can open their bottles; they can buy young wines and have a great pleasure opening quite a young vintage of Bordeaux."

Buy-and-wait losing appeal

As for sales of Bordeaux futures, she said that the region's 2025 en primeur campaign wasn't a pricing failure but a demonstration that fewer collectors want to buy-and-wait.

She said, "Prices have become really attractive in the campaign this year… and there are great opportunities in the 2025 vintage."

"But you can open, say a bottle of 2010, and it will be absolutely fantastic to drink, but for a bottle of 2025, you will have to wait, and even though you don't have to wait for decades, you will still have to wait for a few years before first you get the bottle and then you can open it," she remarked.

While she noted that the 2025 offer for "10 to 20 big names" was "a success," generally the demand for en primeur this year was subdued.

"I think it's really the result, not of a bad pricing campaign – because I think the prices were good – it's more of the trends of consumption: now, there are fewer and fewer people who want to create a cellar, buy wines, wait for years and years before they can buy it," she said.

Concluding on this topic, she commented, "I think the proportion of people who buy a wine, a bottle of wine that's going to be open the same night, is huge. So it's the whole idea of buying which is also which is now in question; I don't think it's a question of price – it's really a question of a habit in consumption."

The best-selling Bordeaux

Meanwhile, below is a reproduction from information from this year's idealwine Auction Barometer on the best-selling Bordeaux in 2025. The web-based business notes that a handful of properties stood out for "striking increases in their volumes". Among these was Château Lafleur (no. 14), which saw its volumes more than double, while its average price dropped to €471 (-25%).

Idealwine wonders whether Château Lafleur's announcement to withdraw from the Pomerol appellation as of the 2025 vintage could have prompted some enthusiasts to part with their bottles, noting that interest in this rare property was strong, though not at any price.

Elsewhere, idealwine noted that Château Figeac (no. 16) managed to "combine a sharp rise in volume (+72%) with only a marginal dip in average price (-3%), confirming the property’s momentum and enduring appeal since its elevation to premier grand cru classé A status for its 2022 vintage onwards".

title: Domaine Lafage steps in to rescue majority of Banyuls and Collioure production
summary:
Domaine Lafage has acquired the struggling Collioure Banyuls Winegrowers' Group (GICB), securing the future of around 60% of production across the two historic Roussillon appellations and creating a new business, Terrasses Vermeilles.

The post Domaine Lafage steps in to rescue majority of Banyuls and Collioure production appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Domaine Lafage has acquired the struggling Collioure Banyuls Winegrowers' Group (GICB), securing the future of around 60% of production across the two historic Roussillon appellations and creating a new business, Terrasses Vermeilles. Domaine Lafage has completed the acquisition of the Groupement Interproducteurs Collioure Banyuls (GICB), taking control of one of the largest wine businesses in southern France after approval from the Perpignan High Court. The business will be renamed Terrasses Vermeilles, bringing together almost 500 winegrowers farming around 500 hectares of vineyards across the Banyuls and Collioure appellations. Based on the 2025 vintage, the new operation represents approximately 10,000 hectolitres of wine annually, equivalent to around one million bottles, accounting for roughly 60% of production across the two appellations.

Safeguarding a historic region

Domaine Lafage said the acquisition is intended to provide long-term stability for growers, employees and customers following months of uncertainty surrounding GICB's future. Jean-Marc Lafage, owner and winemaker at Domaine Lafage, said: "Today is not about victory, but about responsibility." The business said it intends to preserve the historic Les Templiers site, its established brands and the identity of the Banyuls and Collioure appellations, while combining the commercial strengths and distribution networks of both organisations.

Growers at the centre

The new company said supporting growers would be central to its strategy, with plans to improve the value of wines from the appellations and strengthen returns for producers. Domaine Lafage also intends to retain the expertise of GICB's workforce during the transition, describing employees as "an invaluable asset" whose experience will be essential to the business's future. Alongside commercial investment, the company plans to extend climate adaptation work already undertaken across Domaine Lafage's own vineyards to the steep, Mediterranean vineyards of Banyuls. Research into drought resilience, water management and regenerative viticulture developed in recent years will now be applied across the newly acquired vineyards to improve their long-term sustainability.

Long-term ambition

Commenting on the acquisition, Lafage said: "Today we inherit an extraordinary responsibility towards this region, its people and its future. Our ambition is simple: to protect this exceptional heritage while giving it fresh momentum. "We want to pass on appellations that are stronger, more attractive and more widely recognised, both in France and internationally, without ever compromising their identity. "Success can only be achieved collectively. It will depend on the trust of our growers, the commitment of our employees and the support of all those partners who share our conviction that the future of Banyuls and Collioure deserves to be built with ambition."

Building on recent momentum

As previously reported by the drinks business, Domaine Lafage began harvesting its 2026 crop last week, marking the estate's earliest harvest on record after an exceptionally early growing season in Roussillon. The producer has also invested heavily in regenerative viticulture and climate adaptation in recent years, with its entire vineyard estate becoming certified by A Greener World (AGW) at the start of 2026. Techniques including improved water management, biochar applications and agroforestry are now expected to play a central role in Terrasses Vermeilles' long-term strategy.

title: Champagnes & Châteaux adds Brokenwood Wines to portfolio
summary:
The premium winery, known particularly for its Hunter Valley Shiraz, is the first Australian producer that Champagnes & Châteaux will distribute in the UK.

The post Champagnes & Châteaux adds Brokenwood Wines to portfolio appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: The premium winery, known particularly for its Hunter Valley Shiraz, is the first Australian producer that Champagnes & Châteaux will distribute in the UK. In a further expansion beyond its French heartlands, wine importer Champagnes & Châteaux has struck an agreement to distribute Brokenwood Wines in the UK, beginning 1 August. While the portfolio is still led by France, the importer’s range is increasingly international, with producers from across Europe, as well as Argentina and the US. Brokenwood Wines, founded in 1970, now fills an Australian niche in the selection. The Hunter Valley producer’s flagship Graveyard Vineyard Shiraz is one of Australia’s most-lauded single vineyard wines, while its Semillon flies the flag for the region’s ageworthy whites. The selection, however, extends across the Australian mainland. It includes the likes of Margaret River Cabernet Sauvignon, McLaren Vale Shiraz and Yarra Valley Chardonnay, as well as the popular Cricket Pitch range of blends. Speaking about the newly inked deal, Geoff Krieger, CEO of Brokenwood Wines commented: “Champagnes & Châteaux’s reputation for championing exceptional family-owned and independent wine producers makes them a natural fit for our business. “As a Sustainable Winegrowing Australia-certified producer, we take a long-term view of everything we do, from caring for our vineyards to building enduring partnerships around the world.” The UK wine trade will have an early chance to explore the range at Champagnes & Châteaux’s portfolio tasting in London on 9 September. Nathan Hughes, the global sales manager at Brokenwood Wines, will be in attendance. For Champagnes & Châteaux, the agreement represents a growing assuredness in its global portfolio. Founded in 1989, it is a subsidiary of French company Arvitis, which owns key brands such as Champagne Thiénot, Champagne Canard-Duchêne and Dourthe from Bordeaux. The importer currently finds itself in a flurry of activity, with the creation of a new role of off-trade key account manager and “aggressive plans” for Canard-Duchêne. Managing director Charles Taverner, himself appointed less than one year ago, sees Brokenwood wines fitting into the growth-oriented importer. “We are absolutely delighted to represent Brokenwood and look forward to a long and successful partnership in the UK market,” he said. “The wines are of the highest quality; they have a great reputation and perfectly complement our portfolio of independent producers from around the world.”

title: The truth behind pub conversions uncovered
summary:
Pubs are continuing to disappear from Britain’s high streets and, while the sector is enduring challenges, many of the sites are being repurposed by developers. According to new data, pubs are now being converted more than any other building type. db looks at the findings.

The post The truth behind pub conversions uncovered appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Pubs are continuing to disappear from Britain’s high streets and, while the sector is enduring challenges, many of the sites are being repurposed by developers. According to new data, pubs are now being converted more than any other building type. db looks at the findings.

The popularity of pub buildings for property developers

A property analysis assessing more than 800 approved planning applications has recently shown how former pubs, banks, churches, chapels and post offices are being transformed across Britain, uncovering which buildings are most often repurposed and what they are becoming. According to the data, the pub, it appears, is the most frequently targeted for conversion. The research has been derived from planning applications indexed by PlanIt that matched the selected building-type search terms. As the researchers attest: it isn’t a complete audit of every building conversion in Britain, and planning approval doesn’t confirm that the proposed work was completed, but it does unveil what is happening to historic sites on a rapid scale across the UK. Speaking to the drinks business, property buying company Sell House Fast managing director Jack Malnick explained why the analysis began and also what it has uncovered.

A 'significant impact on communities'

Malnick said: "We wanted to understand which forgotten high street figures are most finding new purpose through redevelopment. The findings reflect both the ongoing housing shortage and the challenges facing the hospitality sector. With pubs continuing to close at unprecedented rates, due to rising costs and the lasting effects of the pandemic, it's perhaps no surprise they top the list of repurposed buildings." According to Malnick: “The loss of local pubs can have a significant impact on communities. Many have been part of the local area for decades, serving as important social hubs. The loss of these, often long-standing community pillars, can impact future residents too, with local amenities and high street health boosting an area’s appeal." Almost two pubs a day closed across Britain during the first three months of 2026, according to figures from the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA) and as many as a third of pub losses happen without the required planning permission, according to the Campaign for Real Ale (CAMRA).

Pubs have seen a 20.9% increase in residential conversions

Former pubs account for the highest number of approved or conditionally approved applications in the recent property analysis, with 276 identified since 2021. According to the data, pubs have seen a 20.9% increase in residential conversions between 2021 and 2025. This makes homes the most common new purpose for former pubs, although some have also been converted into retail spaces, hospitality venues, offices, and other uses.

Further pressures making pubs vulnerable

The cost-of-living squeeze continues to reshape spending habits and put pressure on Britain’s high streets, with UK inflation standing at 2.6% in June 2026, meaning household budgets are feeling the pinch and are less likely to spend, forcing businesses to close and creating possible redevelopment opportunities. Rising operating costs, including wages, energy bills and supply expenses, have added further pressure on hospitality businesses - but there is clear appetite for repurposing those buildings and this in itself has become a great to the longevity of the industry and British institutions.

The perfect storm

At the same time, demand for housing continues to remain high, with average UK private rents reaching £1,388 per month in May 2026, up 3.3% year-on-year. This situation has also created the perfect storm for those with closed down venues whereby there is now increased appeal to convert any unused pub buildings into residential properties. Malnick admitted to db that "whilst these closures are undoubtedly a blow to the hospitality industry and community cohesion, it is encouraging to see that vacant buildings are finding new life. According to the data, the majority of repurpose applications are for residential conversions, in turn helping to address the housing shortage". He did however flag that this did not mean that affordable housing was always the outcome, since property development spans a broad range of residences and target demographics with the primary goal for most developers being to make money.

Developers often set out to make money

Malnick explained: "Although it’s unclear how many of these new developments fall under ‘affordable housing’, we remain hopeful that a significant proportion of the residential conversions recorded in our findings meet this criteria." Staying optimistic, Malnick added: “Despite widespread coverage of pub closures, conversions for hospitality businesses were the third most common planning application, behind residential and commercial. This is definitely a positive indicator of investment into local F&B and hopefully an upward trend.”

title: All the medallists from The Global Organic and Vegan Masters 2026
summary:
With sustainability a key issue for trade and consumers alike, organic and vegan wines are gaining in prominence – and quality. Patricia Stefanowicz MW reports. 

The post All the medallists from The Global Organic and Vegan Masters 2026 appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
With sustainability a key issue for trade and consumers alike, organic and vegan wines are gaining in prominence – and quality. Patricia Stefanowicz MW reports.  SUSTAINABLE, ORGANICS, biodynamics and natural wine are the future, according to many in the wine industry. And data shows that vegan is growing too, whether organic or not. The doctrine of sustainability – protection of the environment, economic viability and social equity – is high on the global agenda. Therefore, organically grown grapes and organic wine are a perfect fit. An increasing number of producers and consumers are especially concerned with the first of those ideas – protection of the environment. Climate change is not a myth; it is a global reality. So consumers are looking at ways to help the ecology of the planet. What better way than to eat, and to drink, ‘green’? As many wine producers and wine merchants will attest, it’s not a hard sell. the drinks business is globally renowned for championing the green agenda, so hosting a Global Masters dedicated to organic and vegan wines seems natural. This year’s competition featured a wide range of wines and producers from all over the planet, and almost every style imaginable. There is plenty of excitement from the warmer, drier regions of France, Spain, Italy and Portugal. It is easier to grow grapes without agro-chemicals in these areas. Without quite so many diseases to account for, more natural inputs – and fewer of them, too – are possible. And chemicals, straight from the Periodic Table (copper and sulphur), can control the majority of diseases. Biological controls, such as pheromones or natural predators, are also used, especially against insects.

CLIMATIC VARIATION

Warmer climates in much of the Southern Hemisphere – Australia, South Africa, Argentina and Chile – are becoming more organic. In different, cool climates, the likes of New Zealand and western Canada manage to use organic and even biodynamic viticulture. More surprising, perhaps, is the number of producers in cooler and damper European regions, such as Champagne, Austria, the Veneto in Italy or even England, who are learning how to look after their vines organically. These latter regions are the beneficiaries of so-called global warming. Inevitably, organic wines are just a little pricier than conventional ones, because grape yields are lower and the labour required is more demanding, but, is being greener also being better? Most consumers and winegrowers would answer: “Yes.” What was truly exciting about this year’s Global Organic and Vegan Masters competition was the diverse range of styles and regions featured. The judges were pleased to award Gold medals everywhere and at various price points. Our Master accolades were equally assorted: Champagne Telmont’s Réserve de la Terre Brut, Château Léoube’s Collector Vin de France Cabernet Franc/Cabernet Sauvignon blend, and Feuerheerd’s Colheita Port. However, it was Château Galoupet’s Cru Classé Provençal Rosé that earned the coveted Grand Master title this year. Conscientious consumers and commercial buyers can rest assured: there are plenty of excellent ‘green’ wines to be discovered at reasonable prices. The judges were delighted to be able to reward producers achieving wonderful wines and healthy, living soils.

title: Majestic doubles down on stores with £4m investment plan
summary:
Majestic Wine will invest £4 million in its retail estate this year as the specialist retailer continues to expand its bricks-and-mortar footprint, opening at least four new stores despite continued pressure on the UK high street.

The post Majestic doubles down on stores with £4m investment plan appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Majestic Wine will invest £4 million in its retail estate this year as the specialist retailer continues to expand its bricks-and-mortar footprint, opening at least four new stores despite continued pressure on the UK high street. Majestic has unveiled plans to invest £4 million across its UK store network during the current financial year, beginning with the opening of a new branch in Trowbridge, Wiltshire. The retailer said the programme will fund at least four new stores during 2026/27 alongside a wider refurbishment programme across its existing estate, as it continues to back physical retail as a key driver of growth. The Trowbridge branch, located on Wicker Hill, is the first new Majestic store to open this financial year and stocks more than 1,000 wines, alongside beers, spirits, low and no alcohol products, soft drinks and gifts.

Backing bricks and mortar

Majestic said the investment builds on its strategy since separating from Naked Wines and being acquired by Fortress Investment Group in 2019. Since then, the retailer has opened more than 25 stores across England, Scotland, Wales and Jersey, while refurbishing dozens of existing branches. John Colley, executive chairman and CEO of Majestic Wine Group, said: "Our Trowbridge opening marks the start of another important year of investment for the Majestic business. Our experiential stores and expert colleagues have always been right at the heart of what we do best at Majestic, and they remain a central part of our strategic plan as we expand into new communities across the UK. "This is just the start of our exciting expansion plans for the year ahead, and underscores our confidence in the future of experiential bricks and mortar retail." Each store offers free wine tastings throughout the week, WSET-trained staff and services including wedding consultations, glass hire and Majestic's "No Quibble Guarantee". The Trowbridge branch will also support next-day home deliveries using a dedicated electric van.

Supporting the on-trade

Alongside retail customers, the new outlet will serve hospitality businesses through Majestic Commercial, the group's wholesale arm supplying more than 4,200 pubs, bars, restaurants and hotels across the UK. The business, which was named On-Trade Supplier of the Year at the Drinks Business Awards 2024, counts Manchester City Football Club, Macdonald Hotels & Resorts and Lord's Cricket Ground among its customers. Elizabeth Newman, managing director of Majestic Retail, said Trowbridge had long been identified as a priority location for expansion. "We know there are thousands of discerning wine drinkers in the local community, many of whom already shop with us in Bath, Devizes, Chippenham or online, and our new store will make it even more convenient for them to shop with us," she said.

Continuing investment

The announcement follows continued investment across the wider Majestic Wine Group. As previously reported by the drinks business, the company said in March that it would continue investing across Majestic, Enotria and Vagabond despite proposing a restructuring of distributor Enotria, which included potential job losses as part of a wider strategic reorganisation. At the time, Colley said the group remained committed to investing in "a strong pipeline of new shops and bars" alongside improvements to its logistics, systems and data capabilities, positioning the latest £4 million investment as part of a broader long-term growth strategy rather than a standalone expansion.

title: Why Whitbread’s Beefeater site closures are a forewarning for the sector
summary:
Whitbread confirmed this week that all 106 of its Beefeater restaurants will take place on 10 September. With the group’s Brewers Fayre restaurants also due to close and thousands of jobs across the UK and Ireland being sacrificed, db asks: what should the industry glean from this?

The post Why Whitbread’s Beefeater site closures are a forewarning for the sector appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Whitbread confirmed this week that all 106 of its Beefeater restaurants will take place on 10 September. With the group’s Brewers Fayre restaurants also due to close and thousands of jobs across the UK and Ireland being sacrificed, db asks: what should the industry glean from this? The group, which also owns the Premier Inn hotel chain, first announced that both restaurant brands would close back in April. The move comes as Whitbread is undergoing a major overhaul, cutting thousands of jobs to make £250 million in cost savings in the next five years.

All eyes on Whitbread

Following the announcement, data from Google Trends has revealed that online searches for “Beefeater UK restaurant shutdown” have surged by 5,000%, showing the predicament the company is facing is one that is perceivably courting both panic and intrigue. Indeed, as the sector already faces myriad challenges, the closures all indicate the continued pressures facing the UK's hospitality sector as businesses contend with rising costs and changing consumer demand. Speaking candidly about the Beefeater closures, Liquidation Centre director Richard Hunt, noted that there are key lessons for today's hospitality sector on how businesses can stay relevant and profitable in an evolving and competitive market.

'Businesses cannot simply cut their way to sustainable growth'

Hunt explained that "Whitbread is ultimately making this move in an attempt to save £250 million in costs over the next five years, which demonstrates a proactive effort to protect the long-term health of the business. While reducing costs can significantly improve resilience during challenging trading conditions, it is not a cure-all. Businesses cannot simply cut their way to sustainable growth, they must also continue to attract customers, remain competitive and adapt to changing market trends. If these wider challenges persist, further restructuring may still be required by the company in the future”. Hunt told db that “closing underperforming sites can improve the financial health of a business, but it only creates long-term value if the remaining estate is stronger, more profitable and better aligned with what customers want”. In fact, Hunt reiterated that “the hospitality sector is facing mounting pressure as rising operating costs, changing consumer habits and tighter household budgets continue to squeeze profitability” and noted that “for established restaurant chains, maintaining large estates of physical locations has become increasingly challenging, particularly where sites are underperforming”.

'Adapt' to survive

He insisted that “in today's market, businesses need to continually assess customer demand, monitor competitors and adapt their offering to remain commercially viable”. Due to these struggles, Hunt observed that “the announced closures at Beefeater reflect the wider challenges facing the casual dining industry rather than an isolated issue. Many consumers are eating out less frequently due to the cost of living, while those who do are placing greater emphasis on value, quality and the overall dining experience. Businesses that fail to evolve alongside these changing expectations risk seeing footfall decline over time and become less profitable”. Added to this, he pointed out that “the wider economic backdrop has also played a significant role”. This is because “rising food and energy costs, higher employment expenses and ongoing inflation have all increased the financial burden on hospitality operators”. With this in mind, he said he had witnessed how “even well-known brands are not immune when operating costs continue to outpace revenue growth, making it difficult to sustain less profitable locations”.

Review the business carefully

According to Hunt, “for businesses under financial pressure, the first priority should be carrying out a thorough review of income, expenditure and site performance. Identifying underperforming areas early, renegotiating contracts where possible and improving operational efficiency can help relieve financial strain. If cash flow issues become more severe, seeking advice from a licensed insolvency practitioner at an early stage can help businesses understand their options and, in some cases, avoid formal insolvency proceedings altogether”. Lamenting the loss of the sites and also the livelihoods they supported, Hunt described the importance of hospitality businesses evolving with their audience and core demographic as well as noting how economic uncertainty can have a knock-on effect.

'Essential'

He added: “Closures of this scale inevitably have an impact on employees, local communities and loyal customers. They also serve as a reminder that even long-established household names cannot afford to stand still. Continually adapting to changing economic conditions and consumer behaviour is essential to remaining competitive in today's hospitality market." db reached out to Whitbread for further comment on the closures, but the group has remained silent on the issue.
